promptText: What class of query does pure dense embedding retrieval typically struggle with, motivating hybrid search?
options: Long, multi-sentence conversational questions
Exact identifiers, product codes, error messages, and rare tokens whose surface form matters more than their meaning
Queries written in a language different from the corpus
Queries that contain synonyms of words in the target document
explanation: Dense embedding models compress text into meaning-focused vectors that don't strongly preserve exact surface form, so an embedding model has little reason to place an exact identifier like 'SKU-88213-B' close to documents containing that exact string over other alphanumeric tokens.

promptText: What does BM25 improve upon relative to classical TF-IDF?
options: BM25 removes the need for an inverted index entirely
BM25 caps the benefit of excessive term repetition (diminishing returns) and normalizes more carefully for document length
BM25 replaces term frequency with cosine similarity
BM25 only works on pre-embedded dense vectors
explanation: BM25 refines TF-IDF by saturating the term-frequency contribution so repeated terms don't dominate indefinitely, and by normalizing for document length so long documents don't win purely by containing more words.

promptText: Why can't you simply add a document's raw BM25 score to its raw cosine similarity score to rank hybrid search results?
options: BM25 scores are always negative, making addition mathematically invalid

The two scores live on incompatible numeric scales — cosine similarity is bounded roughly in [0,1] while raw BM25 scores are unbounded and collection-dependent — so a naive sum lets whichever signal has larger magnitude dominate regardless of true relevance
Cosine similarity cannot be computed for text that has also been tokenized for BM25
Vector databases technically forbid combining two different score types in the same query
explanation: A naive sum is effectively dominated by BM25's much larger raw numbers, turning the 'hybrid' system into pure lexical search wearing a hybrid label unless the scores are normalized or a rank-based fusion method is used instead.

promptText: How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combine two ranked lists?
options: It multiplies the raw scores from both lists together
It sums, for each document, 1/(k + rank) across each list it appears in, using only rank position and ignoring raw score magnitude entirely
It always picks whichever list ranked the document higher and discards the other
It averages the two raw similarity scores after z-score normalization
explanation: Because RRF only uses ordinal rank position, not raw score magnitude, it sidesteps the score-scale incompatibility problem entirely, which is why it has become a common default fusion strategy.

promptText: What is the 'vocabulary mismatch problem' that dense retrieval solves but pure BM25 cannot?
options: A query and a relevant document express the same idea with different words (e.g. 'cancel my subscription' vs. 'terminate your plan'), so there is no literal term overlap for BM25 to match on
The query is written in all uppercase while the document uses lowercase
The document contains spelling errors that BM25 cannot tokenize
The query contains stop words that were removed from the index
explanation: Dense embeddings map both phrasings to nearby points in vector space based on meaning rather than exact words, which is exactly the failure mode BM25's literal term matching cannot address on its own.

promptText: In a hybrid search pipeline, if a document appears in the dense candidate list but never appears in the lexical top-N results at all, what happens to it under RRF?
options: It is disqualified from the fused ranking entirely because it failed to appear in both lists
It still receives credit from its dense-list rank alone; the missing lexical contribution is simply treated as zero, not as a penalty beyond that
RRF cannot process documents that are missing from one list and throws an error
It automatically receives the maximum possible fused score as compensation
explanation: Hybrid search is additive insurance, not a strict intersection filter — a document missing from one list simply contributes zero from that list, so implementing hybrid search as 'keep only documents both engines agree on' would be stricter and often worse than either method alone.

promptText: A team narrows the per-engine candidate pool to just the top-5 from each side before running RRF fusion. What risk does this introduce?
options: RRF cannot function at all with fewer than 10 candidates per engine

A genuinely relevant document ranked, say, 20th by one engine (which fusion would have credited) never even reaches the fusion step, effectively starving that signal for queries where it would have found the right answer further down its own list
The k constant in RRF must be recalculated for every query when pools are small
Score normalization becomes mathematically undefined with small candidate pools
explanation: Best practice is to retrieve a wider candidate pool per engine than the final top-K (e.g., top-50 fused down to top-10), since a narrow per-engine pool can silently starve one signal from ever contributing to fusion for certain queries.

promptText: Why is 'atomic ingestion' across the lexical and dense indexes considered a critical operational discipline for hybrid search?
options: Because Weaviate and Qdrant require both indexes to be updated in the same programming language
Because if a document lands in one index but not yet the other, queries return incomplete or inconsistent results with no error raised anywhere — a silent failure mode unique to running two indexes
Because atomic ingestion is required to compute BM25 scores at all
Because dense indexes cannot be updated incrementally without a full rebuild
explanation: Two indexes drifting out of sync — new documents appearing in one but not the other due to a partial ingestion failure — is described as the single most common operational bug in hybrid search deployments, and it fails silently.

promptText: What is SPLADE, and what specific advantage does it retain from classical BM25-style sparse retrieval despite being a neural model?
options: It is a dense embedding model that replaces BM25 entirely and requires an HNSW index
It is a learned sparse retrieval model whose nonzero weights are trained rather than hand-computed, but its sparse, term-indexed output stays compatible with fast inverted-index infrastructure
It is a reranking model that only operates after fusion has already occurred
It is a rule-based synonym expansion dictionary with no learned component
explanation: SPLADE can assign learned weight to related terms that never literally appear in the text (a limited form of expansion), partially closing the vocabulary-mismatch gap, while remaining deployable on the same fast inverted-index infrastructure used for BM25.

promptText: A team tunes their weighted-sum fusion alpha against embedding model A, then swaps in embedding model B with a different similarity score distribution, without re-tuning. What is the likely consequence?
options: Nothing changes, since alpha is independent of the embedding model by design

The previously-tuned normalization and alpha no longer reflect reality, silently under- or over-weighting the dense signal relative to what alpha was originally calibrated for — retrieval quality degrades quietly with no error thrown
The system will throw a dimension-mismatch error at query time
BM25 scores automatically rescale to compensate for the embedding model change
explanation: This is exactly why fusion parameters need re-validation whenever the embedding model changes, and it's a strong argument for using RRF instead, since rank-based fusion has no normalization step that can go stale.

promptText: Why does hybrid search NOT fix problems caused by poor chunking strategy?
options: Hybrid search actively makes bad chunking worse by doubling the index size

If chunks are poorly sized or split mid-thought, both the dense and lexical signal degrade together — hybrid search improves which retrieval paradigm wins for a given query, it does not repair badly prepared source content
Hybrid search only operates on whole documents, never on chunks
Chunking is only relevant to dense retrieval, not to lexical retrieval at all
explanation: This is a common mistake: assuming hybrid search compensates for upstream content-preparation problems, when in fact both retrieval signals are built from the same (possibly poorly chunked) source text.

promptText: How should hybrid search and cross-encoder reranking be combined in a production RAG pipeline?
options: They are redundant — a team should implement only one, never both

Hybrid search cheaply produces a wide, good candidate ranking across two complementary signals over the full corpus, and a reranker then applies a more expensive, more accurate pass over that smaller candidate set — the two compose rather than compete
Reranking must always run before hybrid search fusion, not after
Hybrid search should replace reranking entirely once alpha is well-tuned
explanation: Skipping hybrid search in favor of reranking alone means the reranker's candidate set is already worse to begin with, since dense-only retrieval may have failed to surface exact-identifier matches that hybrid search would have caught.

promptText: An evaluation set for a hybrid search system reports flat aggregate NDCG improvement over dense-only search, leading the team to conclude hybrid search isn't worth the complexity. What is the most likely methodological flaw?
options: NDCG cannot be computed for hybrid search systems at all

The evaluation set likely under-represents exact-match/rare-term queries relative to their real (if infrequent) importance, so hybrid search's concentrated benefit on that segment gets diluted into a near-invisible aggregate number; metrics should be reported per query segment, not only in aggregate
Aggregate NDCG always favors hybrid search over dense-only, so this result must indicate a bug in the fusion code
The team should have used recall@1 instead of NDCG, since NDCG cannot detect any retrieval improvement
explanation: Hybrid search's value is concentrated in a small but disproportionately important query segment (exact identifiers, rare terms); an aggregate metric blending that with a much larger volume of conversational queries can make a real, important improvement look negligible.

promptText: A staff engineer is asked whether fine-tuning the embedding model to better represent exact identifiers would be a better investment than implementing hybrid search. What is the strongest argument for hybrid search instead?
options: Fine-tuning embedding models is technically impossible for exact-match tokens

Hybrid search reuses mature, off-the-shelf lexical technology (BM25/inverted indexes) requiring no training data or corpus re-embedding, whereas fine-tuning requires ongoing labeled data and retraining as new identifiers appear, and risks degrading the paraphrase-tolerance behavior that is dense embeddings' actual value-add
Fine-tuning always produces worse retrieval quality than hybrid search in every measured scenario
Hybrid search requires no additional infrastructure at all, unlike fine-tuning
explanation: Pushing a dense embedding model to also nail exact lexical matching fights against what it's fundamentally built for (semantic compression) and requires recurring retraining and re-embedding costs; hybrid search solves the same problem with mature technology at a lower and more predictable engineering cost.

promptText: A hybrid search system performs well in offline evaluation but poorly in production. Beyond the fusion algorithm itself, what are the most likely root causes to investigate first?
options: The RRF constant k must be wrong, since it is the only parameter that could cause this discrepancy

The evaluation set may not represent live traffic (curated too narrowly or built early in the project), environment differences may exist between the offline harness and production (different pool sizes, stale index snapshot, untested fusion parameters, or caching), and real query/document distribution shift may have occurred since the eval set was built
This gap can only be explained by a bug in the vector database's HNSW implementation
Offline and online metrics are mathematically guaranteed to match, so this scenario is impossible
explanation: This offline/online gap is almost always explained by an unrepresentative eval set, environment mismatches between the test harness and production, or real-world distribution shift — not by the fusion algorithm itself being fundamentally wrong.
